original_value: Self-tracking data is often seen as a means to reflect and achieve a goal, usually focusing on positive insights and actions. Lately, some studies have discussed the negative consequences of self-tracking, suggesting that people interact with personal data in different ways. We explored how self-tracking activities and the emotional context characterize how people engage with personal health data through the analysis of a complex and emotionally-loaded use case: fertility self-tracking. We qualitatively analyzed patient-generated content in an online health community dedicated to fertility. We found five distinct types of engagement with data: positive, burdened, obsessive, trapped, and abandoning. Each of them is composed of an action and an emotional component that mutually influence each other. We discuss how the interplay of these components characterize a person's engagement with data, how the online forum made these issues visible, and how they are embedded in the self-tracking culture. We also provide insights into the implications of these issues for self-tracking tools. Finally, we hypothesize how people transition through the types of relationships with data, suggesting directions for future research in the area.

result.paraphrase: Self-tracking data is often regarded as a way to monitor progress toward a goal, with attention typically centered on positive insights and behaviors. More recently, some studies have examined the negative effects of self-tracking, indicating that people engage with personal data in varied ways. To understand how self-tracking practices and emotional context shape engagement with personal health data, we analyzed a complex, emotionally charged case: fertility self-tracking. We conducted a qualitative analysis of patient-created content from an online health community focused on fertility. Our findings identified five distinct engagement types: positive, burdened, obsessive, trapped, and abandoning. Each combines an action component and an emotional component that influence one another. We discuss how the interaction of these components shapes a person's relationship with data, how the online forum revealed these issues, and how they are embedded in self-tracking culture. We also offer insights into what these issues mean for self-tracking tools. Finally, we propose how people may move between these types of relationships with data, pointing to directions for future research in this area.
